## Video Transcript

## Who was Konrad Lorenz?

If, one day, your parents told you that you were adopted, would you feel differently toward them? If they had raised you as their own, would you love them any less after learning this new information? These same questions are asked in **ethology**, or the study of animal behavior. When animals learn to identify their parents, either biological or otherwise, this is called **imprinting**. **Konrad Lorenz**, considered the founder of modern ethology, was fascinated by imprinting and eventually even earned a Nobel Prize in 1973 in Physiology or Medicine for his work with animals.

## Early Life, Education, & Career

Lorenz was born in Vienna, Austria, in 1903, and, even from a young age, he was fascinated with animals. He would often bring them home and had creatures such as fish, birds, cats, dogs, rabbits, and even monkeys. He even kept diaries on the behavior of birds and provided care for sick animals from the local zoo.

Lorenz's father was an orthopedic surgeon and wanted him to go to medical school. So, in 1922, Lorenz went to Columbia University in New York to study medicine. He eventually returned to Vienna, earning his M.D. and Ph.D. at the University of Vienna. Following this, in 1937, he became a lecturer in animal psychology and comparative anatomy at the same university. He then became professor and head of the Department of General Psychology at Albertus University in Germany and worked there until 1942.

Lorenz served as a physician in the German army from 1942 to 1944 until he was captured by the Soviet army and held as a prisoner of war for four years. After being released and returning to Austria, he served as head of the Institute of Comparative Ethology at Altenberg until 1951. Lorenz later created a comparative ethology department at the Max Planck Institute, eventually becoming co-director and then director. And, in 1973, Lorenz was awarded the Nobel Prize for his work on animal behavior. Lorenz died in his home country of Austria in 1989 at the age of 85.

## Animal Behavior Experiments

Lorenz performed a number of experiments with animals to study their behavior and is best known for his work with erroneous imprinting on young animals. A friend of Lorenz, Oskar Heinroth, initially noticed that graylag geese can attach to humans instead of their mother immediately after hatching. Lorenz was fascinated by this phenomenon, and it led him to experiment with imprinting in order to determine both how this happens and the effects it can have.

In one experiment, Lorenz removed several eggs from a goose's nest. When the eggs hatched, he was the only ''parent'' they saw and knew since they were exclusively in his care. The other geese, from the eggs he left behind, knew only their biological parent. Lorenz's goslings followed him around as if it was completely natural, and even when he mixed the geese up together, they would separate back out to their identified ''parents.''

In a different experiment, Lorenz used a bird called the jackdaw for **sexual imprinting**, which is when an animal learns to identify its mate (as opposed to its parents). What he found was that the jackdaw could be imprinted on so that it tried to mate with species other than its own. Interestingly, though, he also found that animals that are erroneously sexually imprinted upon will not try to mate with the specific individual to which they associate as their parent. In other words, when they were raised by humans, Lorenz could sexually imprint on birds so that they tried to mate with humans instead of birds, but they would not try to mate with him if they identified him as their parent.

Lorenz also learned that there are specific times in a bird's life when different types of imprinting occur. For example, through other experiments, Lorenz was able to alter the behavior of jackdaws so that they would mate with their own species but would fly with crows and eat with humans.

## Learned vs. Innate Behavior

Lorenz believed that animal behaviors are linked to their evolutionary past and, specifically, that aggression is inherited. He argued in his book _On Aggression_ that fighting is an innate behavior that can't be modified. He also believed that fighting occurs between animals because it aids in their survival by keeping competitors spread apart in different territories. Not everyone agreed with Lorenz, though, and this theory sparked some controversy among both animal behaviorists and human psychologists.

In addition to his work with animals, Lorenz also had theories about human behavior and inheritance, as well as family structures. Much of this was drawn from his own experiences. For example, he believed that some fears, like being afraid of snakes, were learned, not innate. He also believed that families should be large so that they provided many extended relatives that could support the children.

## Lesson Summary

**Konrad Lorenz** was an Austrian zoologist who studied animal behavior, or **ethology**. He was specifically interested in **imprinting** (when animals learn to identify their parents), **sexual imprinting** (when an animal learns to identify its mate), and inheritable behaviors. Though he first studied medicine in school, he eventually went on to earn his Ph.D. in zoology. He held many prominent positions at universities and scientific institutions and even won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his work.

Not all of Lorenz's theories were well received, such as his belief that aggression was an inherited trait, but he was very well known for his experiments. In one experiment, he was able to imprint upon geese so that they saw him as their parent. Another resulted in behaviors in jackdaws, such as eating with humans and flying with crows.

## What is Sociology?

In a general sense, sociology can be defined as the study of society and social structures. More specifically, sociologists study human social behavior and the societies and social institutions they create, along with the reflexive relationship between people and society. Often at issue in sociological research are the various ways society and social norms affect people's behavior and, in the same way, how and why people cause social change.

Sociology is regarded as the oldest of the social sciences, a group of academic disciplines that apply social theory and the scientific method to answer questions of social importance. Along with sociology, the social sciences include anthropology, economics, political science, psychology, and often geography and history as well. As the first of these fields of research, sociology shares several traits in common with them. These include the comparison of the past and the present, interest in all levels of society and its development, investigation of a broad range of social institutions, the relationship between people, places, and society, human interpersonal and social communication, and the relation between the individual and larger social forces.

Sociologists take different approaches to research and ask different questions based on the theoretical framework they make use of. Sociological theory is usually separated into classical and contemporary theory, and then further separated into individual theories and concepts. See below:

Classical Sociological Theory (c. 19th century)

*   Structure-Functionalism - Society functions as a unified whole that separate social structures work together to maintain. Research focuses on the specific functions that structures perform. 
*   Conflict Theory - Social conflict is necessary for the creation and maintenance of ociety and for social change to occur. Research is based on the material aspects of social struggle and inequality, and historical change that happens because of it. 
*   Weberian Theory - Individual motivations provoked by disenchantment with the iron cage of society lead to social actions, which help shape society as a whole. Research involves people's propensity for rationalization, and the operation of bureaucracies in society. 
*   Symbolic Interactionism - Social meaning is not inherent to to society, but arises through social interaction, both of which together make up society at large. Research involves individual personalities and social relationships, along with the processes that cause social order and change. 

Contemporary Sociological Theory (c. 1960)

*   Postmodernism - Society is itself a social construct that is divergent and multifarious in theory and practice, and constantly changing. Research involves the various contingent meanings behind social concepts and norms, and the deconstruction of manufactured institutions.
